screens.title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Abstraction reduces complexity by exposing only essential behavior and hiding internal details. In Python we use Abstract Base Classes to specify a contract: methods that subclasses must implement. This chapter shows how to declare an abstract class with the abc module, mark required methods with the @abstractmethod decorator, and prevent accidental instantiation of incomplete implementations. You'll see live code examples that demonstrate the TypeError you get when you try to instantiate an ABC, and then how concrete subclasses like a credit card processor implement the required methods to become instantiable. We'll also compare abstract methods to concrete methods so you can decide what belongs in the contract and what belongs in a shared implementation. Finally, we’ll connect this to Python’s collections. abc interfaces so you understand how ABCs formalize expected behavior for types like Iterable and Mapping. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design an ABC, implement concrete subclasses that satisfy the contract, and avoid the common pitfall of missing an abstract method. Think of an abstract class as a promise — a specification other classes must fulfill — and keep that promise explicit with @abstractmethod.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Abstract Classes and Interfaces
Abstract Classes and Interfaces
Define contracts with abc, then implement them in concrete subclasses.

Abstraction exposes essential behavior and hides implementation. Python's abc module formalizes that abstraction: an abstract class can declare methods without implementing them and require subclasses to provide concrete implementations.

This prevents accidental creation of objects that are not fully implemented. You will see code examples that demonstrate these rules and common mistakes, plus a hands-on Logger activity to practice designing an ABC and two concrete loggers.

Explore Key Topics
Abstraction
Essential vs hidden
ABC & @abstractmethod
Define required methods
Concrete subclasses
Implement the contract
In this lesson: you'll design an ABC, see the TypeError from instantiation, implement concrete processors, and connect ABCs to Python's interfaces.
Visual concept
A contract card shows required methods while helper methods remain implemented.
ABSTRACT
process_payment(amount)
No implementation — subclasses must provide it.
CONCRETE
get_processor_name()
Shared helper with default behavior.
Why this matters
A clear interface makes code predictable and prevents incomplete implementations. Think of the remote control: you press what you need without seeing the engine underneath.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing object-oriented systems in Python. First, you will explain abstraction: how it exposes essential features while hiding complex implementation. An example is a driver using a steering wheel without knowing engine internals. Second, you will understand what an Abstract Base Class is in Python and why it exists. You will learn to inherit from ABC and mark methods with the @abstractmethod decorator so Python enforces the contract. Third, you will implement an ABC using the abc module: writing an abstract class, adding abstract and concrete methods, and observing what happens when you attempt to instantiate an abstract class. You'll practice with the PaymentProcessor example that defines process_payment and refund_payment as required methods. Fourth, you will differentiate abstract and concrete classes by implementing subclasses that satisfy the abstract methods and by recognizing the TypeError that arises when a subclass remains abstract. Each objective ties to a small coding step and a design question, so you finish the chapter able to both reason about abstraction and apply it in code.

screens.title: Abstraction in OOP
screens.narratorSegment: Abstraction focuses on presenting only what is necessary about an object while hiding how it works. A concrete analogy is driving a car: you use the steering wheel and pedals without needing to understand the engine or transmission. In code, abstraction means creating a public A P I or set of methods that clients rely on, and keeping the complicated internals private or separate. This separation gives several practical benefits: it reduces cognitive load for developers using your class, makes it safer to change or optimize internal code without breaking callers, and clarifies the responsibilities of each type in a system. A common misconception is thinking abstraction is the same as encapsulation; they are related but different. Encapsulation bundles data and methods and controls access, while abstraction intentionally simplifies the interface. In Python you achieve abstraction by designing classes that expose only essential methods and, when appropriate, by using Abstract Base Classes to force a contract. For example, a PaymentProcessor defines the required behaviors process_payment and refund_payment. The abstract class does not say how these operations are implemented — it just declares the A P I that concrete processors must provide. Practice by listing the methods a client needs to call and then decide which of those are abstract requirements and which can have shared default behavior. This planning step helps you design robust, extensible class hierarchies.

screens.title: Abstract Base Classes (ABCs)
screens.narratorSegment: An Abstract Base Class serves as a blueprint or contract for a family of classes. It can include abstract methods — method declarations without an implementation — that force subclasses to provide concrete behavior. In Python you create an ABC by inheriting from ABC in the abc module and marking methods with the @abstractmethod decorator. Importantly, an ABC can also contain concrete methods. These shared implementations act as helpers that subclasses may use or override. The crucial rule to remember is this: if a class has any abstract methods not implemented, Python treats it as abstract and will raise a TypeError if you try to instantiate it. This behavior prevents incomplete objects from being created and makes the developer immediately aware of missing implementations. A common pattern is to put only the required A P I in abstract methods and provide default utilities as normal methods, as seen in the PaymentProcessor example where get_processor_name returns a default string. When designing an ABC, ask which methods every subclass must absolutely provide and which can have reasonable defaults. Clarifying that separation early keeps your hierarchy predictable and easier to test.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Abstract Base Classes
What is an ABC?
A class that defines required methods and cannot be instantiated until they are implemented.
How to create one
Inherit from ABC and use @abstractmethod for required methods.
Rule
Missing implementation of any abstract method makes the subclass abstract as well and uninstantiable.
Design tip
Keep abstract methods minimal — they represent the essential contract.
Example snippet
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class PaymentProcessor(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def process_payment(self, amount):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def refund_payment(self, transaction_id):
        pass

    def get_processor_name(self):
        return "Generic Payment Processor"
This ABC declares two required methods and one concrete helper.

screens.title: PaymentProcessor ABC — code
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the PaymentProcessor example. The class inherits from ABC, which marks it as an abstract base class. Two methods are decorated with @abstractmethod: process_payment and refund_payment. These decorators tell Python there is no implementation here and that every concrete subclass must provide them. There's also a concrete method get_processor_name that returns a default string; this method provides shared behavior subclasses can reuse or override. The visual code shows the exact structure: import ABC and abstractmethod, define the abstract methods with pass bodies, and add the helper. A common misconception is trying to provide partial behavior in an abstract method; the decorator means the method is a required contract, not an optional override point. Another point: abstract methods can include a docstring describing expected behavior, which is useful for implementers. When you design an ABC, include clear docstrings for each abstract method telling implementers what inputs are expected and what they should return. That documentation becomes the formal contract. After you write this class, Python will prevent instantiation until concrete subclasses implement both required methods. PaymentProcessor ABC — code means use @abstractmethod to signal required behavior and provide docstrings to document the contract for implementers.. In practical terms, declare abstract methods and a concrete helper. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › PaymentProcessor ABC
PaymentProcessor (definition)
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class PaymentProcessor(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def process_payment(self, amount):
        """Abstract method to process a payment."""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def refund_payment(self, transaction_id):
        """Abstract method to refund a payment."""
        pass

    def get_processor_name(self):
        return "Generic Payment Processor"
Explanation and tips
  • Inherit from ABC to mark a class as abstract.
  • @abstractmethod means the method must be overridden by concrete subclasses.
  • Concrete methods in an ABC provide shared utilities and are optional to override.
  • Include docstrings for implementers to clarify expected inputs, outputs, and side effects.
Common mistake

Trying to instantiate PaymentProcessor directly will raise a TypeError because abstract methods remain unimplemented.

screens.title: What happens when you instantiate an ABC
screens.narratorSegment: When you attempt to create an instance of a class that still contains abstract methods, Python raises a TypeError. This enforcement happens at instantiation time, not at inheritance time, which gives you immediate feedback that the contract wasn't fulfilled. For example, trying to run processor = PaymentProcessor() will produce an error stating that PaymentProcessor can't be instantiated because abstract methods like process_payment and refund_payment are not implemented. This behavior is deliberate: it prevents creating objects that lack required behavior. A common debugging workflow is to read the TypeError message and implement the missing methods in the subclass. Also note that a subclass that implements some but not all abstract methods remains abstract itself. Only when all abstract methods are implemented does the subclass become concrete. Use this rule as a design guardrail: it forces you to complete the essential pieces before running code that depends on them. When writing unit tests, instantiating a subclass will similarly reveal missing implementations early in your test run. What happens when you instantiate an ABC means python raises typeerror at instantiation if any abstract methods remain unimplemented, enforcing the abc contract.. In practical terms, python enforces the contract with a typeerror. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Instantiation & TypeError
Attempt to instantiate
# This will raise a TypeError
processor = PaymentProcessor()

# Example error message:
# TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class PaymentProcessor with abstract methods process_payment, refund_payment
The error lists the abstract methods still missing.
Developer workflow
  • Read the TypeError to find missing methods.
  • Implement all abstract methods in the subclass.
  • Re-run instantiation to confirm the class is now concrete.
  • Use tests to ensure implementations meet the contract expectations.
Misconception

A subclass with missing abstract methods is not an incomplete concrete class — it is still abstract and cannot be instantiated.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › CreditCardProcessor
Concrete class example
class CreditCardProcessor(PaymentProcessor):
    def process_payment(self, amount):
        print(f"Processing credit card payment of ${amount}.")
        return f"CC_TRANS_{amount}_ABC"

    def refund_payment(self, transaction_id):
        print(f"Refunding credit card transaction: {transaction_id}.")
        return True

    def get_processor_name(self):
        return "Credit Card Processor"

# Instantiate and use
cc = CreditCardProcessor()
print(cc.get_processor_name())
cc.process_payment(100.50)
Notes
  • Signature must match the abstract method so Python recognizes it as implemented.
  • Override concrete helper methods only when specialization is needed.
  • Concrete classes enable polymorphism: different processors can be used interchangeably.
Key Takeaway

A concrete subclass completes the contract and becomes instantiable; this is how you provide specific behavior behind an abstract API.

screens.narratorSegment: PayPalProcessor is another concrete implementation of PaymentProcessor. It implements the same abstract methods but with different internal behavior. When you have multiple concrete classes implementing the same ABC, you can treat them polymorphically: code that depends on the PaymentProcessor interface can accept any concrete processor and call process_payment and refund_payment without knowing which implementation it uses. The provided example creates instances of CreditCardProcessor and PayPalProcessor, places them into a list, and loops over them, calling get_processor_name, process_payment, and refund_payment. This loop demonstrates that the same calls work across different concrete types because they fulfill the contract. A misconception is believing polymorphism requires a shared base-class implementation; what matters is the interface. ABCs formalize that interface, and any class that implements the methods correctly can participate in polymorphic code. Use this approach to write flexible processors, test them independently, and swap implementations without changing client code. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Polymorphism with ABCs
PayPalProcessor example
class PayPalProcessor(PaymentProcessor):
    def process_payment(self, amount):
        print(f"Processing PayPal payment of ${amount}.")
        return f"PP_TRANS_{amount}_XYZ"

    def refund_payment(self, transaction_id):
        print(f"Refunding PayPal transaction: {transaction_id}.")
        return True

# Polymorphism demo
cc = CreditCardProcessor()
pp = PayPalProcessor()
processors = [cc, pp]
for p in processors:
    print(f"Using {p.get_processor_name()}:")
    trans_id = p.process_payment(25.00)
    p.refund_payment(trans_id)
Practices
  • Test each concrete implementation independently to verify the contract behavior.
  • Use lists or registries of processors to operate polymorphically in client code.
  • Maintain consistent method signatures to ensure substitutability.
Key Takeaway

Design interfaces once and implement many ways; client code stays unchanged when implementations vary.

screens.title: Abstract vs Concrete Methods
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding whether a method should be abstract or concrete depends on whether you can provide a meaningful shared behavior. Abstract methods represent the essential obligations of the contract — behavior every subclass must implement. Concrete methods in an ABC provide reusable helpers or sensible defaults that subclasses may inherit. For example, process_payment is abstract because each processor has very different steps, while get_processor_name can be concrete because there's a reasonable default value. A useful rule of thumb is: if you can implement a method in a way that fits all expected subclasses, make it concrete; otherwise mark it abstract. Another misconception is converting abstract methods to concrete by supplying a placeholder implementation like pass. That removes enforcement. If you want enforcement, keep the method decorated with @abstractmethod. Document expected return types and side effects in docstrings so implementers know what to return and how to behave. screens.title: ABCs as Interfaces — collections.abc
screens.narratorSegment: Python's collections. abc module is a real-world example of using ABCs to define interfaces. Classes like Iterable, Sized, and Mapping define a set of methods a type should provide to behave like Python's built-in collections. When you inherit from an interface ABC, you commit to implementing its methods and receive the benefit of predictable behavior across the standard library. For example, inheriting from Sequence defines an expected set of methods for sequence-like behavior. The important architectural idea is that ABCs let you specify capabilities, not concrete implementations. Use ABCs when you want to guarantee a type supports operations your code relies on. This approach helps large codebases remain consistent because the interface defines what clients can expect from any implementing class. screens.title: Forgetting to implement abstract methods
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent error is omitting a required method in a subclass and then wondering why instantiation fails. The Device / Light / Fan example demonstrates this: Light implements turn_on and can be instantiated, but Fan, missing turn_on, raises a TypeError when you try to create it. The underlying cause is that Python treats the subclass as abstract until all abstract methods it inherits are implemented. This is not a runtime quirk but a deliberate enforcement to prevent partially implemented objects. To debug, read the TypeError message: it lists the abstract methods still missing. Fix the issue by implementing the method with the correct signature. Another subtle mistake is providing a method with a different signature — for example, missing parameters — which will not satisfy the ABC contract. Finally, avoid relying on protected conventions alone; abstract methods are the explicit enforcement mechanism. Use unit tests that instantiate concrete classes to catch missing implementations during development rather than at later runtime. Forgetting to implement abstract methods means if a subclass lacks even one abstract method or has a mismatched signature, it remains abstract and cannot be instantiated; the typeerror points to the missing methods.. Example from chapter
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Device(ABC):
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    @abstractmethod
    def turn_on(self):
        pass

    def get_name(self):
        return self.name

class Light(Device):
    def __init__(self, name, brightness):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.brightness = brightness

    def turn_on(self):
        print(f"{self.name} light is ON at {self.brightness}% brightness.")

class Fan(Device):
    def __init__(self, name, speed):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.speed = speed

    # Missing turn_on implementation!
Debugging steps
  • Read the TypeError to identify which abstract methods are missing.
  • Implement methods with exactly the expected signature.
  • Add unit tests that instantiate concrete classes to catch missing methods early.
Misconception

Having similar method names or partial implementations does not satisfy the abstract contract; the method must exist with the correct signature.

fullNarratorScript:
Abstraction reduces complexity by exposing only essential behavior and hiding internal details. In Python we use Abstract Base Classes to specify a contract: methods that subclasses must implement. This chapter shows how to declare an abstract class with the abc module, mark required methods with the @abstractmethod decorator, and prevent accidental instantiation of incomplete implementations. You'll see live code examples that demonstrate the TypeError you get when you try to instantiate an ABC, and then how concrete subclasses like a credit card processor implement the required methods to become instantiable. We'll also compare abstract methods to concrete methods so you can decide what belongs in the contract and what belongs in a shared implementation. Finally, we’ll connect this to Python’s collections. abc interfaces so you understand how ABCs formalize expected behavior for types like Iterable and Mapping. By the end of this lesson you will be able to design an ABC, implement concrete subclasses that satisfy the contract, and avoid the common pitfall of missing an abstract method. Think of an abstract class as a promise — a specification other classes must fulfill — and keep that promise explicit with @abstractmethod.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing object-oriented systems in Python. First, you will explain abstraction: how it exposes essential features while hiding complex implementation. An example is a driver using a steering wheel without knowing engine internals. Second, you will understand what an Abstract Base Class is in Python and why it exists. You will learn to inherit from ABC and mark methods with the @abstractmethod decorator so Python enforces the contract. Third, you will implement an ABC using the abc module: writing an abstract class, adding abstract and concrete methods, and observing what happens when you attempt to instantiate an abstract class. You'll practice with the PaymentProcessor example that defines process_payment and refund_payment as required methods. Fourth, you will differentiate abstract and concrete classes by implementing subclasses that satisfy the abstract methods and by recognizing the TypeError that arises when a subclass remains abstract. Each objective ties to a small coding step and a design question, so you finish the chapter able to both reason about abstraction and apply it in code.

Beyond reading, you'll practice by building an ABC and two concrete subclasses. The hands-on Logger activity asks you to design Logger with abstract log_message and close_logger methods, then implement a ConsoleLogger and FileLogger. This practice reinforces the contract: a subclass that fails to implement any abstract method remains abstract and cannot be instantiated. You'll also trace a TypeError example with a Fan class missing its turn_on method, so you understand the runtime feedback that enforces correct design. Assessment items ask you to choose the correct approach to enforce a sensor contract; the right choice is an Abstract Base Class with @abstractmethod. These checks make the concept concrete — you will not only be able to explain abstraction but also detect and fix incomplete implementations. Use the provided code templates as a starter and the safety note to ensure resources like files are closed properly in close_logger. This objective page prepares you for the coding steps and for evaluating if a class is a valid concrete implementation.

Abstraction focuses on presenting only what is necessary about an object while hiding how it works. A concrete analogy is driving a car: you use the steering wheel and pedals without needing to understand the engine or transmission. In code, abstraction means creating a public A P I or set of methods that clients rely on, and keeping the complicated internals private or separate. This separation gives several practical benefits: it reduces cognitive load for developers using your class, makes it safer to change or optimize internal code without breaking callers, and clarifies the responsibilities of each type in a system. A common misconception is thinking abstraction is the same as encapsulation; they are related but different. Encapsulation bundles data and methods and controls access, while abstraction intentionally simplifies the interface. In Python you achieve abstraction by designing classes that expose only essential methods and, when appropriate, by using Abstract Base Classes to force a contract. For example, a PaymentProcessor defines the required behaviors process_payment and refund_payment. The abstract class does not say how these operations are implemented — it just declares the A P I that concrete processors must provide. Practice by listing the methods a client needs to call and then decide which of those are abstract requirements and which can have shared default behavior. This planning step helps you design robust, extensible class hierarchies.

An Abstract Base Class serves as a blueprint or contract for a family of classes. It can include abstract methods — method declarations without an implementation — that force subclasses to provide concrete behavior. In Python you create an ABC by inheriting from ABC in the abc module and marking methods with the @abstractmethod decorator. Importantly, an ABC can also contain concrete methods. These shared implementations act as helpers that subclasses may use or override. The crucial rule to remember is this: if a class has any abstract methods not implemented, Python treats it as abstract and will raise a TypeError if you try to instantiate it. This behavior prevents incomplete objects from being created and makes the developer immediately aware of missing implementations. A common pattern is to put only the required A P I in abstract methods and provide default utilities as normal methods, as seen in the PaymentProcessor example where get_processor_name returns a default string. When designing an ABC, ask which methods every subclass must absolutely provide and which can have reasonable defaults. Clarifying that separation early keeps your hierarchy predictable and easier to test.

Let's walk through the PaymentProcessor example. The class inherits from ABC, which marks it as an abstract base class. Two methods are decorated with @abstractmethod: process_payment and refund_payment. These decorators tell Python there is no implementation here and that every concrete subclass must provide them. There's also a concrete method get_processor_name that returns a default string; this method provides shared behavior subclasses can reuse or override. The visual code shows the exact structure: import ABC and abstractmethod, define the abstract methods with pass bodies, and add the helper. A common misconception is trying to provide partial behavior in an abstract method; the decorator means the method is a required contract, not an optional override point. Another point: abstract methods can include a docstring describing expected behavior, which is useful for implementers. When you design an ABC, include clear docstrings for each abstract method telling implementers what inputs are expected and what they should return. That documentation becomes the formal contract. When you inherit from an interface ABC, you commit to implementing its methods and receive the benefit of predictable behavior across the standard library. For example, inheriting from Sequence defines an expected set of methods for sequence-like behavior. The important architectural idea is that ABCs let you specify capabilities, not concrete implementations. Use ABCs when you want to guarantee a type supports operations your code relies on. One practical benefit is duck-typing with formal checks: isinstance(obj, Iterable) may hold if the class registers with the interface or implements required methods. However, remember the chapter's source: ABCs mainly serve as a mechanism for defining interfaces — they are the explicit contract baked into your type hierarchy. This approach helps large codebases remain consistent because the interface defines what clients can expect from any implementing class. A frequent error is omitting a required method in a subclass and then wondering why instantiation fails. The Device / Light / Fan example demonstrates this: Light implements turn_on and can be instantiated, but Fan, missing turn_on, raises a TypeError when you try to create it. The underlying cause is that Python treats the subclass as abstract until all abstract methods it inherits are implemented. This is not a runtime quirk but a deliberate enforcement to prevent partially implemented objects. To debug, read the TypeError message: it lists the abstract methods still missing. Fix the issue by implementing the method with the correct signature. Another subtle mistake is providing a method with a different signature — for example, missing parameters — which will not satisfy the ABC contract. Finally, avoid relying on protected conventions alone; abstract methods are the explicit enforcement mechanism. Use unit tests that instantiate concrete classes to catch missing implementations during development rather than at later runtime. These key concepts capture the essential takeaways. First, abstraction exposes only essential behavior and hides implementation detail. Use it to design clear, minimal APIs. Second, an Abstract Base Class is a blueprint that can contain abstract and concrete methods; it prevents instantiation until required methods are implemented. Third, an abstract method is declared with @abstractmethod and signals a required behavior subclasses must implement. Keep these ideas in mind when designing hierarchies: declare only the true requirements as abstract and provide shared helpers as concrete methods. Practically, this makes your code easier to reason about and harder to misuse. If you encounter a TypeError about abstract methods, implement the missing methods with the correct signature.
